content: Defense mission and support applications need common XML services within the Defense Information Infrastructure operating environment. The services should let authorized users and applications register shared terms and structures, define reusable XML schemas, and create or consume XML documents. They should also provide vendor-independent access to distributed information so applications can exchange and manage data without depending on a particular physical database implementation.

We’d use it any time different mission or support applications need to share structured data without each one inventing its own format or database interface. That includes registering common terms, publishing reusable schemas, exchanging operational records, and pulling or updating information from distributed sources in a consistent way.
The main thing we’re trying to achieve is interoperability and reuse. We want authorized users and applications to work from the same XML definitions so data can move cleanly between systems, and we want to avoid tight coupling to any one vendor’s database or storage implementation.

Right now, the problem is that different applications often represent the same business data in different ways, which makes sharing and integration slow and brittle. We end up with custom point-to-point translations, duplicate definitions, and a lot of effort just to keep systems talking to each other.
The common XML services are meant to give us a shared, controlled way to define and exchange that data so applications can interoperate more reliably. That should reduce duplication, improve consistency, and make it easier to connect systems without rewriting them for each new interface.

It needs to fit inside the Defense Information Infrastructure common operating environment, so it has to work in a distributed, defense enterprise setting rather than as a standalone application. Practically, that means it should be accessible to authorized users and applications across multiple systems, and it has to respect security controls and whatever hosting standards the environment imposes.
I don’t have the detailed deployment constraints in front of me, but I would expect it to be designed for integration with existing infrastructure instead of assuming a single central database or a specific vendor platform.

Yes, there are likely defense acquisition and hosting constraints we’d have to follow, including approved standards, security accreditation steps, and procurement rules for the environment. My expectation is that we should stay vendor-neutral wherever possible and use whatever XML, interoperability, and enterprise architecture standards are mandated for the DII environment.
I don’t know the exact approved products or the formal approval path yet, so I’d need to verify that with the program and acquisition folks before saying anything definitive.

We should plan for the usual security accreditation and integration review gates that come with deploying in a defense environment, plus any enterprise architecture compliance checks for XML, data exchange, and interoperability standards. The service will likely need to fit approved hosting and authentication patterns in the DII environment, and anything that creates vendor lock-in or depends on a proprietary database interface would be a concern.
I don’t have a confirmed list of preferred or disallowed vendors and products, so I’d need to check the current environment guidance and acquisition policy before naming specifics.

The main situations are when a remote source is temporarily unreachable, a network link is down, or one of the applications consuming the XML service is disrupted but others still need access to shared data. In those cases, we’d want the service to degrade gracefully so users can still retrieve or manage whatever information remains available, rather than bringing everything to a stop.
From a business standpoint, the expectation is continuity for mission-critical exchange and lookup functions, with enough resilience that an outage in one system doesn’t cascade across the whole environment. I’d expect we’d need to clarify which data and transactions are essential to keep available during interruptions and what delay or fallback behavior is acceptable.

For day-to-day use, the basic lookup and retrieval functions need to feel near immediate, because users and applications will treat them as part of normal workflow. Registering new terms, schemas, or structures can tolerate a short wait as long as it completes reliably and gives clear feedback.
I don’t have a formal time threshold to give you yet, but I’d expect interactive reads to be fast enough not to interrupt users, while write or registration actions can be a little slower if that helps with validation and control.

Yes, we’d need to treat the source of truth and freshness carefully, because in some cases a returned XML document has to match the registered definition exactly, while in others a slightly older but still valid version may be acceptable. Partial matches probably make sense only for search or discovery; for actual exchange and processing, we’d want complete and validated results.
If there are discrepancies between sources, I’d expect the system to favor the authoritative registered definition or the approved data source, but the exact conflict-resolution rule would need to be defined.

Authorized users and applications should be able to do it, but not everyone should have the same level of access. In practice, the people who register terms, define reusable schemas, or publish shared structures would likely be a smaller controlled group, while more users and consuming applications can create and use XML documents based on those approved definitions.
Access would be driven by mission role, need to know, security clearance or authorization level, and whether the requester is an approved system or a human operator.

When the XML is being used for official exchange, reporting, or integration with other systems, they should use the authoritative registered definition so everyone is speaking the same language. A local or alternate version might be acceptable only for internal drafting, testing, or isolated use where it is not affecting shared data.
Discovery and reuse should be restricted to what the user or application is authorized to see, especially if the term set or schema is sensitive or controlled. Updates to a registered definition should probably go through the same controlled review and approval path as the original registration, so we don’t end up with conflicting versions in circulation.

Discovery or reuse should be further limited when a definition is still in draft, has export or distribution restrictions, or is tied to a sensitive mission area where only a subset of users should even know it exists. We might also limit reuse if a schema is marked for a particular program or enclave and hasn’t been approved for broader use.
If someone requests an update without approval, the system should not let them modify the registered version directly. It should either reject the change with a clear message or route it into a review workflow, depending on how the governance process is set up.

The main entities are shared terms or vocabularies, reusable XML schemas or structures, and the XML documents or messages built from them. We’d also need to manage metadata around those items, like version, ownership, status, and the approved source.
In day-to-day use, analysts and data stewards would define and maintain the shared structures, while applications would consume them to create, validate, exchange, and retrieve mission data consistently across systems.

When something is drafted, the version should clearly mark it as preliminary, the owner should be identified, and the status should show that it is not yet authoritative. Once approved, the metadata should lock down enough to show who approved it, what the current active version is, and which source is authoritative.
If an item is retired or superseded, the status should change so users and applications know not to use it for new exchange, but it may still need to remain retrievable for legacy reference. If metadata conflicts or is missing, the system should fail safe, meaning it should block promotion to approved status or flag the item for manual review rather than guessing.

We need to preserve the ability for existing systems to keep exchanging data without disruption, especially the mission-critical ones that already depend on current repositories or message formats. It’s also important to preserve legacy access to older definitions and documents so teams can still support historical data and interfaces during the transition.
What matters most is that users can find the right approved definition, systems can validate and process XML consistently, and we don’t create a lot of manual rework or downtime. The transition should improve control and interoperability without breaking what is already in operational use.

If the content is still actively used in operations and can be mapped cleanly, it should be transformed into the standard XML structure so it can participate in the managed environment. If it is already XML and matches the approved model closely enough, then converting it as-is may be fine, but only if it validates against the registered definition.
If the content is obsolete, too ambiguous, or not needed for ongoing business use, it should be kept only as retained historical reference. The deciding factors would be operational value, conversion risk, and whether the content can be governed and reused without introducing errors or inconsistency.

A smooth experience means authorized people can quickly find the approved term or schema they need, register a new one without a lot of manual back-and-forth, and know exactly what version is current. For systems, it means they can validate and exchange data against the managed definitions without custom handling for each source.
Day to day, success looks like fewer integration issues, less duplication, and clear governance so users don’t have to guess which XML artifact to use. If something is not approved, they should get a clear reason and a path to fix it rather than just hitting a dead end.

They would use the shared XML services when a new mission term needs to be standardized, when a program wants to publish a structure others can reuse, or when multiple systems need to exchange operational data without each one maintaining its own private format. It is appropriate when the data has broader reuse value, needs governance, and benefits from a common authoritative definition.
It would not be appropriate for ad hoc local data that is only relevant to one system and doesn’t need to be shared or controlled centrally. If the exchange is temporary, highly experimental, or too sensitive to expose beyond a closed application boundary, then using the shared service may not be the right fit.

The practical rule is whether the item has ongoing enterprise value and can be governed safely. If it is needed only inside the source system, it should stay there; if it is useful more broadly but contains sensitive details, it should be masked or summarized before publication; and if it has no reuse value or cannot be handled safely, it should be excluded from the managed XML environment entirely.
The key test is whether exposing it would add mission value without creating unnecessary risk or operational burden. If it fails that test, we should keep it out of the shared environment.

Only designated data owners, schema stewards, or other approved program representatives should be able to publish or update reusable schemas and managed documents. Before those assets become available, they should pass validation against the registered rules, review for correctness and consistency, and an approval step that confirms the content is ready for enterprise use.
If the change affects shared terms or interfaces, I would expect a stronger review, possibly with governance or configuration control approval. The main point is that no one should be able to make something broadly available just because they have technical access.

At minimum, it should move from draft to under review to approved or rejected, with the ownership, version, effective date, and classification metadata populated before approval. The system should also record who submitted it, who reviewed it, and when the status changed so there’s a clear audit trail.
If metadata is missing, conflicting, or out of date, the asset should not be promoted. It should be flagged back to the owner for correction, and the system should prevent release until the required fields are complete and consistent with the current authoritative records.

Once an asset is in use, any correction or update should go through controlled versioning rather than overwriting the approved one in place. The system should keep the current approved version available for users, mark the revised one as pending review until it is approved, and preserve the old version so existing integrations do not break unexpectedly.
If an asset is retired, it should be clearly marked as deprecated with guidance on the replacement if there is one, and the system should stop new use while still retaining it for traceability and historical reference.

We would want a phased rollout rather than a big-bang release. My expectation is that it starts with a limited pilot for a small set of trusted users and systems, then expands to additional programs once the core registration, approval, and exchange functions are stable.
I’m not sure yet whether there is a formal sequence already mandated, but that kind of staged deployment would be the safest approach for this environment.

I would expect the schemas and terms to evolve gradually as missions change, new data needs show up, and existing definitions get refined for clarity or interoperability. Interfaces may also need to expand, but ideally in a backward-compatible way so current consumers can keep working while they adopt the new version.
Those changes should be introduced through versioned releases, with advance notice, clear migration guidance, and a deprecation period before anything old is removed. That way existing users are not forced into an immediate change, and systems have time to adjust on their own schedule.

At the outset, the main problem is that different defense applications are each managing their own XML definitions, terms, and data exchanges, which causes duplication, inconsistency, and extra integration work. The service needs to give them one controlled place to register shared structures, reuse schemas, and exchange XML data without tying anyone to a specific database implementation.
I’d say the first release is successful if a pilot set of systems can publish and consume approved XML assets through the service with less custom point-to-point work, and if the shared definitions stay consistent across those users.

An XML document should be accepted only when it conforms to the approved schema and uses the managed terms and structures exactly as defined for that version. It should be rejected if required elements are missing, values are out of range or wrong type, or it references an outdated or unsupported definition.
When source data does not conform, the service should return clear validation errors and keep the document out of the approved store until the issuer corrects it. If we can map parts of the data safely, that’s useful for assistance, but I’d still expect the nonconforming document to be blocked from being treated as valid.

Once retired, I’d expect the asset to be removed from normal selection for new work so users cannot accidentally keep adopting it. If there is a replacement, the service should warn and redirect users to that newer approved asset; if there is no replacement, it should clearly indicate that the asset is retired and should not be used going forward.
It should still remain searchable for audit, traceability, and historical reference, but with a retired status that makes its lifecycle state obvious.

The service should provide enough metadata to make the choice obvious, like the asset’s purpose, owner, version, approval status, and any known replacement or dependency. I’d also expect guided selection, meaning the default view should surface the approved, current version first and explain why it is the recommended one.
For onboarding, it would help to have plain-language descriptions, sample payloads or usage notes, and validation feedback that tells a new integrator what they did wrong and how to fix it. The goal is to let someone new find the right artifact without already knowing the internal history.

Approved artifacts should show the full, current metadata and usage notes, with sample payloads that match the active schema exactly. Deprecated artifacts should still show their historical details, but the display ought to make the status very obvious and discourage new use, while replacement candidates should be presented as the preferred option with a clear link back to what they supersede.
I’d also hide or minimize anything that could confuse a new user, like obsolete examples or unsupported fields, unless they are needed for migration or audit purposes.

For official exchange, reporting, and integration, users and systems should only be allowed to discover and use the authoritative version. Local or alternate versions can be available for internal drafting or staging only if the user has the right permissions, and they should be clearly labeled as non-authoritative so they can’t be mistaken for the approved standard.
If the content is sensitive or controlled, discovery should be limited even further so only authorized roles can see that the alternate version exists at all. In practice, I’d expect the service to enforce both access control and status-based rules, so the wrong version cannot be selected for formal use by accident.

The practical rule should be based on whether the item is needed beyond the source system and whether it can be exposed without violating policy or mission need. If it is temporary or highly sensitive and has no approved sharing purpose, it should stay in the source system; if some shared use is needed but the raw content is too sensitive, it should be masked or summarized before publication.
If it cannot be sanitized to an acceptable level, then it should not enter the managed XML environment at all. In other words, usefulness to other authorized users has to be balanced against classification, privacy, and operational risk.

I’d expect any change to a managed definition, schema, term set, or document to be audit logged, along with who did it, when, what changed, and what version was affected. Access events should be logged for sensitive items, approvals, rejections, retirements, and any permission changes, because those are the actions we’d need to trace later.
For bulk or system-generated activity, I’d still want logging, but probably at a summarized level with enough detail to reconstruct what happened without flooding the audit store. The only real exception would be routine background processing that never changes managed content and does not touch sensitive data, and even then I’d want that exception documented.

The local version should be reusable only when the user is explicitly working in a draft, test, or internal context and has permission to use non-authoritative content. In that case, the system should keep it marked as local or variant so it does not get promoted or treated as the approved standard by default.
If the reuse is for an official managed process, then only the authoritative version should be allowed unless there is a documented exception and approval path. That keeps people from accidentally building operational workflows on something that is merely convenient but not sanctioned.

Only in rare cases where the authoritative version is unavailable, not yet published, or explicitly exempted for a specific mission need should a non-authoritative version be selectable for formal use. That exception should require an approved waiver or designated authority sign-off, and the system should record the justification, scope, and expiration of the exception.
Even then, the non-authoritative version should be clearly flagged in the UI and metadata so downstream users know it is not the standard. Once the authoritative version exists, the exception should automatically stop being the default choice.
